title: Donald Knuth
concept: Zero-based indexing: ArrayList and Python list indexes run from 0 to size()-1; mixing 0- and 1-based conventions causes off-by-one errors
alt: xkcd comic: one programmer tells another he is being inconsistent with his array indices, some starting from one and some from zero. The other replies that different tasks call for different conventions, and quotes algorithms expert Donald Knuth as saying “Who are you? How did you get in my house?” — which is what Knuth said when he asked him about it.
caption: Java and Python have already picked a convention for you: the first element is at index 0 and the last is at size() - 1. Mix the two and you get an off-by-one bug — and no need to break into a professor’s house to settle it.

title: Linked List Interview Problem
concept: Linked lists: each node holds only a next link, so a singly linked list can be traversed forwards but never back
alt: xkcd comic: at a coding interview, asked to traverse a linked list, a candidate writes a function on the whiteboard that emails the list’s head pointer to a technology museum as an item donation. The interviewer says “Hey.” Caption: Coding interview tip: interviewers get really mad when you try to donate their linked lists to a technology museum.
caption: Each node knows only its next — which is why, in the hover text, Randall won’t traverse this list himself: a singly linked list never shows you the way back.

title: Workflow
concept: Programming to an interface: declare List<T> and rely only on what List promises, not on one implementation's accidental behaviour
alt: xkcd comic: a software changelog for version 10.17 reads “The CPU no longer overheats when you hold down spacebar.” A long-time user complains the update broke his workflow, because he holds spacebar instead of the hard-to-reach Control key and configured his editor to treat the rapid temperature rise as Control. The admin replies “That’s horrifying.” Caption: Every change breaks someone’s workflow.
caption: He relied on something the software never promised. Write List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); and use only what List promises, and swapping in a different implementation later won’t break anyone’s workflow.
